maintopic: CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PRIVILEGE ON COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Canada Evidence Act by inserting therein new sections to extend a privilege on communications between members of the public dealing with members of the clergy, the medical profession and social workers acting in their professional capacities. This is in accordance with the report of the committee on privileged communications to the Ontario civil justice subsection of the Canadian Bar Association.
The common law already confers a privilege from disclosure with respect to communications passed between a client and his solicitor. The rule is stated in Cross "Evidence" (1957), page 238.
The study and recommendations made by the Canadian Bar Association with respect to privileged communications have been spurred by the opinion expressed by Hon. Mr. Justice Stewart during the course of the trial in the case of Dembie v. Dembie in April, 1963. Mr. Justice Stewart expressed the opinion very clearly that a certain communication between i patient and her psychiatrist should be privileged from disclosure. However, there svas no formal ruling made by the trial judge is to whether the communications previously referred to were privileged. Therefore, quite tpart from the effect of the doctrine of prec-:dent, the learned judge's opinion cannot be considered as a ruling which has become embodied in the law.

maintopic: QUESTIONS

speechtext:
1.	Did the government receive a submission from the council for laboratory animals dealing with the subject of the protection of animals used in scientific research and, if so, when was such submission received?
2.	Does the government plan any action in this session with regard to the matters raised in the said submission?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: PROTECTION OP ANIMALS USED IN RESEARCH
speechtext:
1 and 2. Yes. A submission was received by the Minister of Justice and Attorney General in July, 1963, and in September, 1963 was passed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for consideration. The views of the interdepartmental committee which had been formed in 1961 were sought. It was generally agreed that no agency of the federal government had authority to institute licensing or inspection over the control of laboratory animals handled by universities or private interests engaged in research work. It was also agreed that legislation establishing any such system would not be within the legislative power of the federal parliament but rather of the provinces. The Minister of National Health and Welfare directed that all laboratories in her department follow as a standard the code of treatment for laboratory animals which was adopted by the Canadian federation of biological societies and indicated that consideration would be given to having that code, or some mutually agreed

new code, adopted to ensure humane treatment of animals in all laboratories operated by the federal government.

I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if I might reply to a number of questions that were put to me on Thursday and Friday of last week in connection with the student loans legislation.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni raised some questions about credit unions, and in particular I believe asked why they had not been included in some of the publicity that was arranged in connection with this program. I should explain that the main source of the detailed information on the plan which was prepared for the public is a brochure which has been given very extensive distribution. This brochure explained that some credit unions are expected to make arrangements to provide loans under this plan. It is, therefore, not correct to say that all publicity in connection with the Canadian student loans plan omitted any reference to credit unions.
A number of advertisements in newspapers and by radio across the country just prior to and following the Labour day week end were 20220-522J
Inquiries of the Ministry primarily designed to draw the attention of students to the fact that loans were available. At that time arrangements for the designation of credit unions as lenders had not been completed, and the advertisements did not specifically mention credit unions.
The letter to which the hon. member referred in his question took issue with the omission in a recent brief television interview in connection with the Canada student loans plan. In my reply to this letter I pointed out that a credit union may be designated as a bank under this act. I assured the league that I am fully cognizant of the important role played by credit unions in the field in which many of them have done pioneer work. In this connection hon. members will be interested to know that a first group of credit unions will be formally designated as banks for the purposes of the Canada Student Loans Act some time this week.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I think it was on September 17, asked if I would table or make available the different quotas for each of the provinces. Hon. members may recall that on July 14, 1964 I gave the house approximate figures for the provincial allocations. The final figures for the loan year ending June 30, 1965 were sent to the provinces on August 21, 1964. They are as follows: Newfoundland, $1,176,000; Prince Edward Island, $232,000; Nova Scotia, $1,736,000; New Brunswick, $1,416,000; Quebec, $12,964,000; Ontario, $12,440,000; Manitoba, $1,968,000; Saskatchewan, $1,908,000; Alberta, $2,852,000; British Columbia, $3,236,000; Yukon, $24,000; Northwest Territories, $48,000.
The hon. member for Athabasca asked a question in respect of the allocation to students in the Ottawa area. As I explained last Thursday, whatever regional limits there may be within a province on the amount of loans available to students are set by the provinces and are outside my jurisdiction. In this connection I have been advised by the Ontario authorities as follows:
In Ontario, because a large number of institutions were named as issuing agencies, authority was given to each institution to issue certificates of eligibility up to an initial specified amount. Such a procedure was necessary in order to ensure that, in total, the 44 issuing agencies did not exceed the provincial allocation. The individual allocations were made on a proportional basis and for institutions in the Ottawa area the initial allocations totalled $830,000.
In the letter of instructions sent by the minister of university affairs to each institution it was stated:
8238	HOUSE OF

No final limit has been set for any Ontario institution. If any institution in Ontario finds its initial allotment temporarily inadequate to meet demand, it should communicate with the department of university affairs as it has been directed.
The final question on this subject was asked by the hon. member for Hamilton South. He asked whether I had received representations from the Canadian union of university students requesting a supreme court ruling or a test case on the Canada Student Loans Act and, if so, what had been my reply. The answer is that I have received no such representation.

I wonder if I might take this opportunity to deal with a question on another subject which was asked on Friday of the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. speechtext: Will it be government policy to bargain with the provinces to see to it that any extension of the tax abatements or transfers from the federal treasury to provincial treasuries will go hand in hand with a continuation of the reciprocity and national uniformity provisions?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS CONTINUATION OP PRESENT PROVISIONS RESPECTING SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: In answer to that question I would call attention to the work to be done by the tax structure committee which was set up jointly by the federal and provincial governments, as has been reported earlier. I do not, therefore, wish to say that the federal government will take a positive decision until we have the benefit of the report or recommendations of this joint committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me about a report that appeared in the Winnipeg press to the effect that an Indian child has been mistreated in a boarding house in Winnipeg. I have now had a chance to investigate this matter, through my officials, and should like to advise the house as follows.
I am informed that it is not correct to state that children are placed in foster homes in Winnipeg that have not been investigated. Following discharge from hospital, it is often necessary to find a boarding house for an Indian child pending arrangements for transportation and escort to his home in the north, or sometimes to continue with his medical treatment as an out patient. Some of the homes so used are licensed by the city of Winnipeg as boarding homes for children. Where these are not available, placements are supervised by departmental officials. We are informed that short term boardings are not necessarily licensed by the province or by the municipality and, as I have said, where such licensed homes are not available, placements are made and supervised by our departmental officials. These officials, because the children have just left hospital, are in almost constant daily contact with the children and their temporary homes.
In this particular instance we had previously placed children in this home. The woman in question had satisfactorily cared for five children in the last six months for periods of from two weeks up. There was no evidence of any previous mental history and no knowledge of mental instability on her part. The selection of homes which my department makes in regard to these Indian children is confined to married women with children who maintain homes and children in a satisfactory manner and have suitable accommodation for short term boarder placement. After an initial visit by a member of my departmental staff, periodic visits are made and the condition of the children during the stay and on leaving the boarding house is noted.
When the little girl in question was discharged from the children's hospital on April 2, 1964, she was taken by a member of our department to the home of Mrs. K. Wall. On
Inquiries of the Ministry April 9 the department's Winnipeg office was notified by her husband, Mr. Wall, that the infant had fallen out of the top bunk bed and had been taken to the children's hospital emergency ward by Mrs. Wall.
One of our medical officers immediately investigated and was told by hospital authorities that the child's injuries were not consistent with the story told of their having resulted from a fall. Therefore immediate action was taken to notify various authorities and to have an investigation undertaken, which resulted in referral to the attorney general's department for police investigation.
The hospital's social service department then visited the home in question to persuade this lady to voluntarily accept psychiatric help. This was done on a voluntary basis before the case came up in court. It is very deeply regretted that the baby in question has sustained what is apparently permanent mental injury, but I know of no way in which any of my officials might have known in advance that this could possibly happen, or could have avoided it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO MEET NATIONAL PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on these occasions the opportunity is given to members of the house to place before the country matters upon which, in the opinion of the opposition, the government has failed to discharge its responsibilities.
The motion in question is one which goes back to the earliest days. I am going to mention the purport of the motion, because frequently it is misunderstood. It is a principle of our constitution that the House of Commons shall control the finances of the country. For almost 550 years that right has been asserted in varying degrees, until within the last 200 years it has been fully confirmed and is no longer subject to dispute. In other words this motion provides the opportunity- and I quote from citation 234 of Beauchesne's fourth edition-for asserting that:
The ancient doctrine that the redress of grievances should be considered before the grant of supplies is maintained in the House of Commons of Canada.
The motion permits a wide discussion, and a discussion in the House of Commons which

is not limited by the rules. In fact the decision of Speakers throughout the years has been that members may discuss various questions on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair, and a great latitude is allowed on these occasions.
I do not intend to speak at very great length today, Mr. Speaker. Some 17 months have gone by since the present government took office, and what has taken place in the intervening months causes one to read with interest the views expressed by the Prime Minister in his address to the nation on the day after the change of government. These words will take their place with other words uttered by those who will always regret having done so. These words, grandiloquent in their construction, provided a promise and a blueprint which in the light of experience will be either condemned or approbated. He said:
The task ahead then is immense hut it is not frightening. It is complex beyond simple description, but it is not impossible. It will not be an easy time, but it will, I pledge you, be a time to excite the daring, to test the strong and to give new promise to the timid. It will indeed be a time of direction and decision, where our efforts are sustained, our purpose clear and our faith high.
Mr. Speaker, those words as a guide to the government were great in their conception, and have been awful in their execution. I am sure even the most patient supporter of the government must laugh inwardly when he thinks of those words and the degree to which this government has failed in the implementation thereof.
Your Honour, as everyone knows there are six of these motions provided by the rules. In the month of May we passed up one opportunity to debate the motion. So far there have been three motions. On April 20 the amendment moved to the motion was that this house deplored the announced decision of the government to abandon its responsibility for the administration of veterans hospitals. The next amendment to supply motion was made on May 4 having to do with a co-ordinated national water policy, and suggesting the establishment of a national advisory committee on water resources and an acceleration of the application of ARDA policies, the expanding of water and other resource development programs conceived and established by the previous Conservative government. That motion, while defeated, in light of subsequent events has proven to have been an understatement.
The next motion was made on May 25, and the amendment was:

This house regrets the continuing failure of the government to take effective action with regard to the pressing agricultural problems of eastern Canada.
That situation is the same today as it was then, with the perambulating Minister of Agriculture being everywhere but in the House of Commons while the problem for the farmer in eastern Canada becomes worse and worse. An example today had to do with the turkey industry. When the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary referred to the situation in respect of that industry all he received was the same old push-off on the part of this government.
Those three amendments in the light of subsequent events have been shown to have been well founded, irrespective of the votes that took place in the house. Under the rules two days are provided for debate and there is still one more motion to come up, though there has been an informal agreement entered into-which is as equally as binding as if it were formal-that supply motion No. 6 will not be proceeded with because of the desire of hon. members to get on with the business of the house.
These motions give the opposition an opportunity to analyse the shortcomings, weaknesses, failures and retreats of the government in the administration of the affairs of the country. Of course the limitation on discussing those matters is that we should not be too general but should particularize. Sir, there have been so many failures on the part of this government in 17 months that any catalogue of unfilled promises could result in an amendment being moved that would be longer than any other moved in the history of parliament. Unfilled promises and uncertain and fumbling courses have made a mockery of the words of the Prime Minister in April, 1963.
Sir, we have a government that seems to have no compass, no sense of direction and no chart but that of expediency; a government whose slogan might well be tax and tax, spend and spend, retreat and retreat. That has been the history of this government, and no particulars are necessary. The evidence is apparent in every department of government. This is a government of indirection that, for some reason known only to itself, with the exception of one or two matters that have been before the house, has been so confused with legislation so ill conceived that it either has had to withdraw what it had advanced, amend what it had decided upon or repair and amend the orig-
Alleged Failure to Meet National Problems inal plans placed before parliament. It is a government that nationally has failed to bring about anything approaching national unity. It is a government that has failed to deal with the centrifugal forces that threaten the unity of Canada. It is a government that in 17 months has brought about greater divisions in this nation than had ever been seen or could possibly have been imagined since confederation. In every department it is a government that has been weak and inefficient, dawdling and uncertain, and has failed to bring before parliament legislation covering those matters that are necessary. It is a government that has increased taxation; a government that, at a time when taxation should be reduced, is taking the very opposite course.
Mention has been made today of the sales tax on production machinery and on building materials. Sir, no other nation in the western world imposes such taxes, yet this government going contrary to every economic advice it would receive from those who are experienced in the civil service of the country, brought in that tax while we in the Conservative party stood against it. It has paid off as far as revenue is concerned. I have not the latest figure, but the information I have available indicates that in January the total tax was $8.2 million, in February $7.5 million, in March $11.4 million, in April $10.3 million, and in May $13.4 million. Those are taxes imposed on progress in this country.
We took strong objection to this and continue to do so. Almost every economic and business organization in Canada has condemned this tax, but the government has refused to act. The total amount collected in 1963-64 was some $62 million. I have told the house what the figure was up to the end of May.
What has this tax done? It has simply been a clog on development. It is all very well to talk about the great expansion in building and the like, but when you deduct from expenditures 8 per cent tax that is now in effect the jubilant figures that are put forward become less optimistic in their effect. And so I could go on throughout the entire picture of development on the part of the government.
We believe the time has come for a substantial reduction in taxation. We said during our period of office that Canada was on the upgrade, that the economy was on the way up, but those gloomsters opposite said "nothing of the kind". Now they admit that 45

Alleged Failure to Meet National Problems months ago the Canadian economy started to rise. Furthermore, they ridiculed us when we brought into effect the pegging oi the dollar which induced and brought about a tremendous expansion in our trade. Ridiculed when in opposition, it has now become the cornerstone ol their policy when in office.
With regard to the field of trade, the Minister of Finance, having secured a great victory in convention on Saturday-he is better in conventions than he is in parliament- dealt expansively with the economy. I should like to have heard him on the question of trade. I should like him to tell the house and the country why it is that in the field of trade our imports are increasing at a substantially greater rate than our exports. I should like him to tell us what the situation is as to the balance of payments. Certainly Canadian producers and manufacturers are having more and more difficulty competing, operating as they do with the load of the tax on production machinery. These are things upon which information should be available. These are things that optimistic statements cannot brush aside.
I mentioned a moment ago something of the situation with regard to Canadian unity. Can you imagine a government which sets up a committee for the purpose of looking into the effects of separation? I know the Prime Minister stated he really did not have that in mind, but I am going to read from Hansard of June 26 last where, as found on page 4780, he was asked whether he would con-sides- a study being made of the economic social and political effects on the rest of Canada of separation, in view of the need for clarification of this subject. The Prime Minister replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have been considering the matter. It is not a subject which lends itself to easy investigation and dogmatic conclusions, but officials of the government are making that kind of investigation now.
There can be no misunderstanding there, and the same position was repeated the other day in the house. When everything should be done to bring about unity in the nation, this government admits to a spirit of defeatism by setting up a committee of civil servants to look into the effects of separation. And so on in the whole picture.
I mentioned agriculture in eastern Canada. I could deal with the field of unemployment and how the government was going to meet that problem. All that was needed was for them to take office and unemployment would disappear. That was the undertaking. We do


not hear much about unemployment today in spite of the fact that it is at a very high level. We hear little or nothing about that. This is the party that promised much in every field of endeavour.
This cursory outline would indicate that if we were to move an amendment to cover the shortcomings of the government we would have one lengthy and filled with detail, for in every sector of government there has been failure. I look at these giants opposite and think of what they promised. I am not going into the record of the campaign promises of 1962 and 1963. I am simply mentioning one or two matters which indicate the situation. They do not know where they are going. They start, they go forward, they retreat. In almost everything they do they emulate the man on the flying trapeze. Oh, there is plenty of action. You see them moving, and then they go back. That has been the story of the present government.
We have been criticized for bringing in amendments. Many have said, why bring in amendments because you know what the result will be? The government has allies, and those allies stay with the government whenever there is a challenge in the form of an amendment. At least, they stay with it to the extent that will assure that whatever the amendment may be, however well founded it may be, it has no possibility of acceptance. That has been the story throughout the picture.
We have been criticized for moving amendments knowing they would be defeated. We know that whatever amendment we might move today, we could expect it to receive the same treatment that all amendments, however beneficial, have received in the past. In addition, we want to get on with the business of the country. We do not want to hold up the government. We have examined a great portion of the estimates during discussions on interim supply. We are most anxious that all departments of the government shall be opened so the necessary examination may be completed at the earliest possible date. All we want is to get the departments before the house, and we will deal with them effectively and I hope efficiently. We do not want to delay. We just want to help the government get these estimates before the house so that we can discharge our responsibilities.
We have had to wait for a long while since the last motion of this type. We want to have the opportunity to look into these

matters. We have no confidence in the government, but to move an amendment would, on the basis of past experience, be a continuing experiment in hope without expectation.
We therefore take this general stand. We have made clear the fact that we have no confidence. The record of the government has been one of uncertainty and worse. There are great issues. We are waiting for the pension bill; when will it come? Well, you remember that when the first one came in, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said this is the finest thing ever. She said, "If you do not pass it, you will not have me." We did not get the opportunity, and we still have not. Then there was the second edition. There is a third edition now in drydock. Eastern agriculture has been forgotten by the government. The government has done nothing but borrow and apply cur ARDA program, then carry it out with less effectiveness than it deserves. There has been no action to assure new hope for eastern agriculture. All the way across the picture there is the same attitude. Northern development is down to a trickle.
In every field of operation we have seen this uncertainty, this failure to grapple with problems. This action of bringing in the flag was taken in order to cover up the government's failure in so many other fields of endeavour. We have seen all that. It needs no amendment to establish it; we simply state our case.
I mentioned a moment ago that there has been criticism about the moving of amendments. We have been asked, why do you move amendments? Well, it is a course that good parliamentary procedure usually dictates. We find, however, it is being interpreted as a desire to bring about an election. We do not want to be misinterpreted. It has been explained also by a certain leading front bencher that these amendments prevent the government from grappling with problems. If only the opposition were not there, what they would do. We want to give them the opportunity at once to bring in the departments that are not before the committee as yet, so they can be examined.
Before I sit down, let me repeat that the fact we have not moved an amendment does ncrt mean we have changed our attitude in any way. It simply means we are trying to bring about the effectiveness of which the Prime Minister spoke. We want parliament to come to grips with the estimates so we can get them out of the way. Having said that, I conclude.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important that the business of the house be not unduly delayed, and as far as I am concerned, I shall hardly delay it for more than a few minutes. However, I feel that we cannot allow certain statements to go unanswered and that we have to establish a certain policy with regard to our concepts.
Mr. Speaker, everything the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) just stated with regard to this government is valid. When he blames this government for increasing taxes, I cannot but support him. When he blames this government for its continual retreats, I cannot but support him; when he upbraids this government for the economic situation of this country at this time, I cannot but approve him; and when he criticizes this government for its indecision and continual retreat, I have to support him.
But there is another thing I want to add. When the Leader of the Opposition was head of the last government conditions were worse than those we know today, or at least as serious.
When the two old parties are in power we see perpetual tax increases; we see indecision and feel a general economic disorder. Indeed, we may well remember the economic situation in 1959, 1960 and 1961, when the present Leader of the Opposition was in office. At that time things were far from being rosy. Taxes were very high, as was the number of unemployed.
The present Leader of the Opposition, who was then prime minister, was well known for his inability to take decisions.
Mr. Speaker, when in opposition you criti-icize the government's decisions. That proves
824G	HOUSE OF
Alleged Failure to Meet National Problems one thing: when the two old line parties, Whig or Tory, Liberal or Conservative, are in opposition they claim that they can do everything and blame the government. But when they are in office they are no longer able to do anything except increase taxes, increase unemployment, show more indecision and preside over a disastrous economic situation for a country as wealthy as ours.
On many occasions in the last few weeks the Leader of the Opposition has been talking as if the third parties were the allies of the government. Now if we look up the Votes and Proceedings of the house and especially the votes taken in the course of the last 12 months, we note that the principal friends or allies of the government are not the third parties but rather the members of the Conservative party, because when there is an important vote we note that there are nearly always 30, 35, 40 and even 45 conservative members absent.
Indeed, I remember that on the occasion of an important vote, when barely 12 more votes would have upset the government, I could not keep from mentioning in this house that if the 40 Conservative members absent at that time had been present in the house the government would have been defeated.
In this case, who is the principal ally of the Liberal government?
A short time ago, I think it was in Charlottetown, the leader of the Conservative party stated that the Ralliement Credi-tiste always followed the Liberal party. Let him figure out the number of votes taken in this House of Commons since he has been in opposition, the number of times the Ralliement Creditiste voted against the government and the number of times the Conservative party voted with the government compared with the number of times the Ralliement Creditiste did. I think that he will be surprised to find that his party voted with the government more often than the Ralliement Creditiste ever did. Let the leader of the Conservative party base his information on figures and then he will stop referring to third parties who are the allies of the government and realize that, on the contrary, his own party is the first ally of the present government.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the statements just made by the leader of the Conservative party concerning the spirit of indecision and retreat of the present government. However, when one realizes that it is the same thing when either of the two old parties is in
[Mr. GregoireJ

power, one cannot help note a very important point, and it is this: Canada needs and must choose a new government, formed with a new party and not with those two old parties we have had since confederation. They have not succeeded in giving our country an economic, political and social system that would enable this nation to develop completely and fully with all its resources and potential. Indeed, they only succeeded in administering the debt in terms of taxes, economic slump and unemployment as we have at this time.
I maintain that Canada will have to call on new ideas, a new system, a new organization of the development of our natural resources, if we really want to have a full development.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned a while ago the existing divisions in Canada. It may be true that there is some dissension, but I feel the ones who are mostly to be blamed for that are still those who would like to continually raise the English against the French or the French against the English although there is room for both ethnic groups in this country.
The Leader of the Opposition is probably one of the persons largely responsible for the disunion now existing, not only in the country but also within his own party. He has succeeded in creating within the Conservative party an image of the same disunion now existing all across the country. You do not have to look far to find out who is responsible. You only have to look at his own chair to see one of the first persons responsible.
As far as we are concerned we declare that there is room for everybody in Canada, for all groups, and even the smaller groups who came to settle in this country. There is room for all those who want to live in peace with other citizens, without trying all the time to blame one another, but rather allowing everybody to develop fully in harmony, while partaking in the country's wealth. We believe that there is room for all by respecting the rights of all and giving freedom to all and the possibility to develop.
The Creditistes maintain that it is possible to achieve that purpose, but in order to do so it is essential that we change the main basis on which confederation stands at the present time. We want to remake the constitution and confederation according to new principles. That does not mean to tear everything down and destroy everything; that means to give a new direction to what exists now, and direct

confederation thanks to a new constitution, so that the present discord might be eliminated.
This dissension is found even within the Liberal party. A Liberal minister, in Quebec, says something and that creates dismay in the ranks of the federal Liberal party. Why? Yet, they are two Liberal groups, but they can no longer agree. It seems that the turn of mind of a Quebec Liberal changes when he is elected to parliament in Ottawa. If he is a man of real ability, as there are some in the cabinet at present-several Liberals have personal, intellectual and moral merit-it seems that as soon as he sits on the front benches, he immediately disregards his ideas and principles and thinks only in terms of the party line. On the other hand, if he has no merit, a Liberal member or any old-line party member who comes to Ottawa simply remains silent and does not bother to express any views or principles.
We see, as an example-I regret that he is not in the house at present-the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) whose opinions were quite different before he came to parliament in Ottawa. Now, he is confronted by what he previously condemned, that is Ottawa and co-operative federalism, and he is discarding what he previously preached, he is sacrificing his ideas and his principles to his party's interests.
That has happened ever since 1867 within the old political parties which have governed this country.
The Creditistes believe that these dissensions could be terminated and that peace could be restored. That would not be difficult to achieve as long as confederation could be reestablished on a new basis.
The essential basis-this has been said often, but I want to repeat it, in the hope that the present government, which realizes more and more that the present situation is getting tense and the atmosphere heavier all the time, and parliament will try to do something before it is too late-is to recognize not only in parliament and in speeches, but also in practice, that our country is made up of two different nations which can live together, not necessarily apart but in close association, to make Canada one of the greatest and most prosperous countries. Two associated states each having its own responsibilities, and reaching an agreement on a number of others. Two associated states are not separate states, on the contrary, they cooperate instead of being divided.
Alleged Failure to Meet National Problems
We are advocating the principle of two associate states and this is the present tendency. If parliament-I do not mean the government but parliament-if all members of the house agreed to draw up a new constitution: two associate states in certain common fields which would keep their responsibilities in certain others.
We are now witnessing on the contrary, the continuous intrusion of the federal government in provincial fields, when the federal government should feel duty bound to respect the rights, obligations and responsibilities of provincial governments. Two associate states which would work together in certain fields, but which would leave to the provinces a certain number of other fields.
We have drawn the list of 16 different fields including defence, external affairs, atomic energy, an agency which now exists, and also transport and postal service. In short, there are 16 different fields where two associate states could co-operate through a really non-federal government and not a government trying to control both states within confederation. This can be done.
Then, the association of two states would develop peacefully and would enable both states to develop more extensively. I have seen citizens from other provinces, even important men in the political field, who desired more and more centralization, a central government, whereas Quebec province and the people wished exactly the opposite. By adopting the principle of two associate states, there would be decentralization for those who want it and centralization for the others. Both states could develop more fully than they are now doing.
Mr. Speaker, we will have to come to such an association some day, for confederation, as it exists now, cannot continue to make progress, because there are only compromises, half solutions, false solutions, solutions that do not settle anything.

Second, there were similar incentives, together with a three year tax exemption, for manufacturing and processing enterprises establishing new facilities in areas of slow growth and high unemployment. As most hon. members know, this has provided a stimulus to the manufacturing industries of this country which, except perhaps during the last war, they have never had to the same degree. the second reading of Bill No. S-35, to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act was passed in April 1962 and became effective January 1, 1963. The legislation provides for the reporting of financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of corporations and labour unions carrying on activities in Canada. The purpose of the act was described at the time of its introduction to produce certain statistical information on the operation of the economy, the extent of foreign control, and effects of this control. In the course of the debate on this legislation in April 1962, the minister informed the House of Commons that the present form of the legislation was to some extent experimental, that there was a recognition of the importance of good relations with suppliers of data and that amendments to the legislation would be introduced in the light of experience. The amendments that are now before the house carry forward these assurances. The amendments, which affect mainly that portion of the act applying to corporations are designed first, to eliminate a substantial burden to some 30,000 large and medium-sized corporations who at present have to provide virtually the same financial information to the dominion statistician and the Department of National Revenue, and second, to eliminate duplication by these two separate government bodies, that is the dominion statistician and the Department of National Revenue, by establishing an integrated collection and tabulation procedure.
As will be recalled, the information on corporations collected under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act is separated into two clearly defined classes. The first class includes information on directors and share ownership and is available to the public. This 

class of information would remain unchanged, except that the amendment will facilitate the reporting of information on the distribution of outstanding share capital by permitting this information to be reported as of any specified date within three months before the end of the fiscal year rather than at the end of the fiscal year only. Corporations frequently prepare this information for their own purposes as of dates prior to the fiscal year-end and this amendment is intended to allow a single tabulation by the company to meet the requirements of the act as well as of the corporation. This information is available to the public, and will continue to be available.
The second class of information reported under the act relates to financial statements and certain specified payments to non-residents. This financial information is confidential and is available for government use only. The remainder of the amending legislation applies to this class of information.
As previously indicated, the financial statements required by the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act are virtually identical with those submitted to the Department of National Revenue for corporation income tax purposes. Shortly after the act was proclaimed it was provided by regulation that a copy of the latter statement, as filed with income tax, could be filed with the dominion statistician as compliance with this portion of the act. This provision, while it helped respondent companies, did not fully satisfy them and suggestions were received from many firms that a single financial statement, the one received by the income tax authorities, should be used instead. To accomplish this, two changes are proposed in the present amendment. One of the amendments is designed to provide for the same certification arrangements under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act as under the Income Tax Act. The other is designed to provide that corporations have complied with the requirements of the act, as far as financial statements are concerned, by submitting financial statements to the Department of National Revenue for taxation purposes. Other information now required under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act-payments to non-residents and the information on directors and share ownership-would be submitted through the Department of National Revenue at the same time.
The amending legislation envisages also a single tabulation operation to meet the needs of both the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of National Revenue after

financial returns are submitted to Ottawa. The Department of National Revenue now examines, punches and tabulates information on about 28,000 companies for its own purposes and in order to publish the annual volume known as "Taxation Statistics". The staff of the dominion statistician is required to do the same under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act for about 30,000 companies, most of which are the same companies. An integrated operation has obvious advantages. The resulting combined data, as contemplated by this legislation, will be prepared on a single consistent basis, avoiding a degree of confusion which it would otherwise be difficult, perhaps impossible, to avoid. In addition to an annual report as required by the legislation, the dominion statistician would assume from the Department of National Revenue responsibility for preparation and publication of the corporation portion of the annual report, to which I have referred, "Taxation Statistics". This integrated program is made possible by giving the dominion statistician access to national revenue corporation tax returns, and this is one of the main purposes of the act.
Access by the dominion statistician to these tax returns calls for special measures to preserve the same sort of secrecy of corporation tax returns as now exists. This involves repealing that section of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act which now gives officials of government departments access to financial statements under certain specified circumstances. The question naturally arises as to whether this is a serious loss. It appears to the government that the advantages of this arrangement considerably outweigh its disadvantages. In fact, during the one and a half years that the legislation has been in effect access to individual corporation records has not been necessary, and need by government for information has been satisfied by summary tabulations. It may be that access to individual company statements might be useful at some future time, but against this must be weighed the annual reporting cost and inconvenience to some 30,000 reporting corporations. Experience suggests, moreover, that less burdensome procedures could be used to meet these needs, and if members be used to meet these needs, and if members of the house would like some further information about this when the bill is before the committee I will be very happy to suggest what those alternative procedures might be.
I should state, in conclusion, that the amending legislation has been developed after 20220-523J
Corporations and Labour Unions Act careful study by the Department of National Revenue and the dominion bureau of statistics in consultation with other interested government departments. The present burden of duplicate reporting had given rise to many complaints and to suggestions from the business community that the returns required under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act and under the Income Tax Act should in some way be consolidated. As I have already indicated, the proposed amending legislation will eliminate a burden to business, eliminate duplication in government departments, facilitate more effective processing of corporation financial statistics, and free resources to produce more comprehensive and detailed statistical studies and analyses which, in line with the purposes of the act, will throw added light on the operations of vital areas of the economy. Furthermore, these amendments do not in any way impair the information on directors and share ownership made available to the public under this legislation through the Secretary of State.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill appears to be very innocuous, but I should like to point out to the house that its implications are far greater than the minister has led us to believe. I think that the last two questions put by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) have pointed this up. In any event, I agree there was a fundamental departure with the introduction of this legislation in 1962, and I think at that time there were certain people who, frankly, were a little dubious about it and had reservations.
The legislation was effective from January 1, 1963 and already we have certain amendments being put forward on the basis of the introduction of a bill in the other place. With regard to the first class of information required under part A concerning shareholdings and so on, I dare say there are some advantages in having a degree of flexibility so that the shareholdings shall not be those listed on the last day of the fiscal period. The question of whether the period should be three months, 60 days or only one month is a matter for decision, and perhaps on the basis of experience a period of three months was found to be more flexible. I have no further reservations with regard to that point except that I think a period of three months does allow for certain changes to take place which might otherwise be shown in the intervening period.
However it is with regard to the second class of information to which the minister has referred that I part company with him. We are being asked this afternoon to underwrite what is really administrative convenience. There is an inviolate principle of confidentiality with regard to income tax returns. We know that in other sectors it takes an order of the court to bring about the production of an income tax return. Corporations, like individuals, are entitled by law and by tradition to confidentiality of their income tax returns.
The information that is sought in part B is the same fiscal information which the company is required to file under certain safeguards of secrecy. The minister said it is virtually the same information supplied in the income tax return, but it is not the same information. In that regard I should like to


have the minister define just how "virtually the same" it may be. What is the degree of similarity between the return filed with the Minister of National Revenue and that required to be filed with the dominion statistician?
I can understand quite readily that a corporation may be prepared to file a second copy of its income tax return with the dominion statistician voluntarily and may signify its willingness to do so, but for the law to say that its income tax return shall be the equivalent to the return required to be filed under part B and that the dominion statistician shall have the right to enter into the records of the Minister of National Revenue with regard to corporations and extract the required information from those returns is another thing. In addition, not only is the dominion statistician to be authorized to examine the income tax return for the information now required under part B, but this amendment will authorize the dominion statistician to examine any and all information, relevant and otherwise, filed by a taxpayer. My colleagues point out that I may have created a little confusion. I mean a corporate taxpayer, because after all we are not talking about individuals here.
But why is this being done? The minister indicates that the purpose is to introduce an integrated operation and that the dominion statistician will now take over the preparation of the annual statement of statistics compiled by the Minister of National Revenue and which is prepared by his officials in summary form. Any taxpayer knows that the information on which it is based is absolutely inviolate so far as secrecy is concerned. We are being asked to authorize another individual or officers under his jurisdiction to enter into the Department of National Revenue.
Already we find a great reluctance among the general public to answer questions with regard to the census because they fear that another government department may have access to this information and may create some difficulties. This reluctance on the part of the individual often leads either to a refusal or to difficulties with the census taker. If for the purpose of integrating operations under the act under consideration at the present time, the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, and the Income Tax Act we are going to allow the dominion statistician to have access to corporate income tax returns, then I say this is more than the thin edge of the wedge. If today it is the dominion

statistician, tomorrow it may be another individual in the government service. I cannot see why-I have great reservations about this-for reasons of administrative convenience, we are extending or derogating from the principle of the confidentiality of income tax returns.
I wonder why it is found that so many concerns have expressed objection to the filing of this information; yet they do. They object also to supplying statistics for the Unemployment Insurance Act or the Statistics Act. This is another return for the government. Parliament has decided that this information dealing with the degree of foreign control of corporations and other related matters should be available. It is information which would otherwise have to be obtained by examining income tax returns. The previous administration, I think, respected the principle of the confidentiality of income tax returns. In my opinion they acted rightly. If a corporation, however, wishes to give a copy to the dominion statistician for the purposes of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, that is its own decision. It waives the secrecy of its own return. However, these amendments take away the secrecy of these returns, although they do clothe the accessibility with a certain degree of secrecy.
These amendments, Mr. Speaker, go beyond what was indicated by the minister's presentation. It is not only the return that is to be filed with the Minister of National Revenue which would be deemed to be a statement filed for the purposes of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, but it gives access to further documents and further information. In other words, under the proposed amendment the dominion statistician can wade through, willy-nilly as he desires, all sorts of returns and information filed by a corporate taxpayer. I do not believe this is right, and I am opposed to this sort of thing.
I think myself that if we are going to have acceptance of the continuation of a principle of confidentiality of income tax returns, it should be extended to the corporation as well as the individual. Why should it be respected for an individual and not a corporation? There are many men in business on their own who are quite as successful and earn just as much as, if not more than many corporations. However, nothing is being asked of them; their returns are to be left alone. Under these proposed amendments we create two categories of taxpayer in so far as the secrecy of returns is concerned. I do not believe that
Corporations and Labour Unions Act is right. A man in business on his own, who may be very successful, should be in the same position as a corporate taxpayer; or vice-versa, the corporation should be in the same position as the individual in so far as the inviolability of the tax return is concerned.
I myself am not satisfied with the explanation of the minister. I must say that I would much prefer to hear a clearer and more detailed reason as to why this rather extraordinary step is being taken. I can see that it will be a nice, neat package, or it would appear to be so, from an administrative point of view. But where do we stop administrative convenience at the expense of the rights of individuals, be they persons or corporations? I am quite anxious to hear the minister reply to these few remarks. I think any further remarks I have to make will be made at a later stage in the debate, depending on the decision of the house with respect to these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, there are three things I want to say about this bill, second reading of which is now before the house. It is always risky for a speaker to say in advance how many things he wishes to say because he may think up other things as he goes along. However, to begin with there are three things I want to say.
First, I am disappointed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) in introducing this legislation did not give us something in the nature of a report on the act which it is proposed to amend. I think he should have told us whether it has been found to be worth while. I think he should have told us what its purposes are and whether or not those purposes are being realized. In fact I think he should have posed
8264	HOUSE OF
Corporations and Labour Unions Act for us the question whether or not the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act should be continued at all. I shall return to that point later, but for the moment that is the first heading I have in mind this evening.
The second observation I want to make is that unless the minister can persuade me otherwise it looks as though the amendments proposed in Bill No. S-35 are discriminatory-in favour of corporations as against trade unions. Perhaps I should develop that point right now. The main purpose of these proposed amendments, as I understand it from the remarks of the minister and from reading the bill, is to simplify the task which corporations face in completing and compiling the returns called for under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. The main way in which this simplification is to be achieved is by permitting corporations which make returns under the Income Tax Act to be excused from making similar or comparable returns under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. This looks very innocent on the face of it, but what it does is to bring the kind of information which corporations are required to file under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act within the secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act.
There is no suggestion anywhere in this amending legislation that the same privilege is to be accorded to the trade union movement. Rather, the whole amending bill deals with corporations and, as I see it, it allows them a cloak of secrecy with regard to this information which they do not now possess. That, it seems to me, is contrary to the whole spirit of the original act as it was brought in by the previous government. After all, the whole purpose of that act was to bring to light certain things which were of concern to the previous government. That is being forgotten and there is an element of discrimination in what the government now proposes as a remedy. I do not know whether "remedy" is the word. It is a concession to firms which have found it awkward or onerous to supply this kind of information.
The third comment I wanted to make is that I cannot weep any tears with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) because there may be some invasion of the inviolable secrecy of the Income Tax Act as far as the corporations are concerned. This of course to the hon. member for Edmonton West, and no doubt to hie friends, amounts to invading the holy of holies. As hon. mem-


bers know, many years ago I did in fact introduce a bill to amend the Income Tax Act so as to remove the veil of secrecy from corporate income tax returns when information filed in that way was sought in either of the houses of parliament. So I do not think the Minister of Trade and Commerce need pay too much attention to the criticism which has been made of this legislation by the hon. member for Edmonton West and which, no doubt, will be made by other members of the Conservative party if they speak on second reading of this bill.
As a matter of fact-and this comes under at least two of the headings I have in mind tonight-I am surprised that the hon. member for Edmonton West, who belonged to the party which was in power when this legislation was brought in, should wish to clamp down a veil of secrecy. After all, the whole purpose of this legislation was to find out what the story was with respect to the influence of foreign entities, either corporations or trade unions, in the economic life of this country. I hear the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) telling me quietly that I have misinterpreted what the hon. member for Edmonton West had to say. If I have done so I will be glad to correct what I have said. But the concern which the hon. member for Edmonton West is showing for the secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act is a concern which somehow gets shown with particular feeling when corporations are involved.

That gives me the right to disregard the rules against repetition and point out to him that the amending bill being brought in by the Minister of Trade and Commerce permits corporations under this act to file their information under the Income Tax Act instead of under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, and therefore to take advantage of the stricter secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act. But that right is not accorded to trade unions. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that is an element of discrimination that should not be introduced.
May I go back, however, to the first point I made and say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that I hope when he takes advan-

tage of the opportunity that will be his to close the debate on second reading he will tell us something about this act. After all, he was not here when it was passed, but I do not think his party, in opposition at that time, was very enthusiastic about it. Surely the minister must have some idea as to whether it is worth having on the statute books; as to whether it is worth all the trouble to which it puts both corporations and trade unions, in order to get this information. I agree with the minister that it is good to have information. I may point out, Mr. Speaker, that when the Canadian Labour Congress spoke against the enactment of this legislation even before it was proposed, it made clear that it was in favour of the collection of all information necessary for the efficient running of our economy. But 1 suggest that the purpose of this legislation was more than just an academic interest in the collecting of information. Indeed there was at least in part a malicious intent in the legislation.
I think we should be told by the minister who is responsible for the branch of government that is administering this act whether anything of use has come to light during the time this information has been collected. I believe we should be told whether anything has been proven by the collecting of this information. The minister told us-and other figures that we have substantiate it-that some
29,000	or 30,000 corporations are filing returns. He told us that at the present time both the dominion statistician and the Department of National Revenue are punching cards to compile all this information. In addition to that we know that about 100 international unions and about 50 national unions are filing the same information and that all this information has to be punched, compiled, computed and tabulated.
We are for information being obtained. We think we should have all that is necessary. But is this information necessary? Is it providing anything? Is it being helpful? Let me put it another way, Mr. Speaker: is any information being obtained as a result of this legislation and all the work that goes into carrying it out that is not obtained in other ways? On the side of the corporations, is not all the information that is obtained under this act obtained either through the operations of the Income Tax Act or through the publishing by corporations, under the requirements of the Companies Act and other legislation, of their annual financial statements?
Corporations and Labour Unions Act
I ask the same question with regard to trade unions, both international and national. Is not all the information that is obtained by the operation of this act made public already by the annual statements that international and national unions publish in connection with their conventions, which they hold freely and openly throughout this country?
I come back to the position taken by the Canadian Labour Congress when this legislation was first brought in. The congress, through its officers, appeared before the government of the day on February 2, 1961, and noted that the speech from the throne that had just been given disclosed that there would be legislation introduced along the lines of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. The congress at that point said that of course it would have to wait to see the legislation before it would make detailed comment; but it did say this, which I think still holds-and I am reading from the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress to the government of the day on February 2, 1961:
We would like to comment, however, that there are important distinctions to be made in the matter of disclosures as between business and labour organizations. As you are undoubtedly aware, to a very large extent the financial and other affairs of foreign-owned subsidiaries in Canada remain very much matters known only to the foreign headquarters of these subsidiaries. Such subsidiaries, while physically located in Canada, may be so controlled from abroad and so manipulated as to operate contrary to rather than in the Canadian interest. It is obviously desirable, therefore, that the veil of secrecy which surrounds their operations should be removed and that the people of this country should know at least as much about these subsidiaries as they are able to learn about Canadian-owned public corporations.
It might be argued that the legislation as it was put upon the statute books in part at least met that desire. If it did, that is being detracted from now by the opportunities corporations will have to file their returns in such a way that they will be under a strict veil and cloak of secrecy. Let me read another paragraph from this 1961 brief of the Canadian Labour Congress:
For international trade unions, the case is somewhat different and we are inclined to take exception to the coupling together of business and labour organizations since to our mind they cannot be so readily equated. But the record will indicate that there is far less secrecy about the operation of international unions in Canada than is the case with international corporations. The constitutions of our unions are open to scrutiny to anyone who cares to examine them. Almost all unions nowadays publish detailed financial statements in a way which makes them available to the public as well

Corporations and Labour Unions Act as to their own members. Union conventions are held openly. In fact, there is no institution in Canada today which has been so minutely scrutinized in recent years as the trade unions, and the public's ability to do so rests largely on the fact that there is little or no secrecy attached to union activities. We are therefore not likely to upset readily any legislation which will interfere with the internal affairs of the trade unions by making mandatory what is already done voluntarily, or by imposing rules and regulations for the conduct of trade union affairs which more properly should be done by the unions themselves. The century-long record of the trade union movement in Canada does not warrant any legislative interference.
It might be said that this was the view of the Canadian Labour Congress when all it had was warning in the speech from the throne that this legislation was coming. It might be said that body should have waited until the bill had come to light. I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that after the bill had been introduced and passed, and during the time when it had not yet been proclaimed, the Canadian Labour Congress appeared again before the former government -this was on December 11, 1962-and had this to say about the very legislation which then had been passed and which we are now being asked to amend:
We have on two previous occasions referred to the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. We have expressed strong criticism of it. We have challenged it on grounds of principle as well as for technical reasons.
A fresh examination of this legislation has served amply to confirm the feelings we already had. We are persuaded that the act, to the extent that it affects trade unions, will Impose on them unnecessary and onerous burdens in the matter of reporting a variety of kinds of information. This will be a hardship for smaller unions in particular but may seriously impede the legitimate activities of all unions. A great deal of paper work will be involved and it is altogether possible that unions will find it necessary to make constitutional and other procedural changes in order to satisfy the requirements of the act. In addition, the ambiguity or lack of clarity of some of the provisions gives us further cause for apprehension.
That was the view of the Canadian Labour Congress about this legislation after it had been passed. That was part of the brief presented to the former Conservative government on December 11, 1962. In the very next paragraph there is a sentence in which the congress urged the government of that day not to proclaim that legislation. That request that it be not proclaimed was made on December 11, 1962, and the response of the former government was that it was proclaimed effective January 1, 1963. In any case it was the view of the Canadian Labour Congress that this legislation as far as trade unions are concerned was not necessary, and that any infor-

mation required from trade unions was readily available. Nothing is being done in this amending bill to make the situation less onerous for trade unions; as far as corporations are concerned it is being made less onerous, and as part of the bargain they are also given the means whereby the information supplied can come under the veil of secrecy which obtains under the Income Tax Act.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that instead of the casual introduction of these technical amendments which the minister gave us he should have told us quite frankly whether in his view as a Liberal cabinet minister this legislation is necessary at all, and I hope that at the end of the debate on second reading he will tell us what he failed to tell us at the start of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, sitting as close to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as do the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and I, it is hard to understand how the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could have so completely misheard what my colleague was saying this afternoon. Our objection to the extension of the powers of the dominion statistician to inspect the income tax returns of companies is not that it protects the companies concerned; it is that it puts into the hands of the dominion statistician unnecessary information which could be misused. Beyond that, it could also inhibit the operations of this particular act. If a company voluntarily submits the information to the dominion statistician, as it would do to the income tax authorities, then that is all right. Our objection to these amendments is that they will not make the operation of this act more efficient.
It seems to me that the explanation given by the minister this afternoon was rather casual and slight. I am not even sure that he had his heart in it, because at a certain stage of his explanation he rather tried to suggest that this bill was merely an extension of Conservative legislation. I am sure that if he was proud of it he would not have made that concession. Actually that is not so: This bill is not an extension of our legislation.
I think that before this debate closes we should have a considerably fuller explanation of the amendments than we have had. For example I would want the term "virtually identical" explained. I think we should have a complete explanation of what is required by the dominion statistician and what is required under the Income Tax Act. I am wondering whether the amendments are not being made

an excuse rather than filling a need. The minister says that many corporations have objected to filing these returns. Most people in varying degrees object to making returns to the government. Every time one makes out another form he says: "What the so-and-so am I doing?" I am wondering whether that is the kind of objection to which the minister refers and whether the people interested in extending bureaucratic control have not seized on this rather general objection to specifically widen bureaucracy in the government.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says that this legislation is loaded in favour of permitting the companies to become more secretive, thus rendering this particular legislation less effective. I do not think that is the purpose, but if it is we should know about it. We should also know whether or not the corporations, through their organizations, are in favour of it. We have heard nothing from the minister about what the various tax associations and other business organizations feel. Perhaps rather than dealing with the matter now this bill could be referred to our banking and commerce committee, and if these organizations wanted to make representations the opportunity would then be given them. We could also hear representations in a general way from the Canadian Labour Congress and other labour organizations.
It seems that the more one looks at this the greater are its implications. I think it would be dangerous just to slip this legislation through as routine, having been blandly assured that it is merely an extension of former legislation. I feel that rather than an extension of former legislation it is changing the course of that legislation, the purpose of which was to make public certain matters. Under the amendments those matters which were to be made public are perhaps going to be made secret.
