Mr. Speaker, I should like to review the original course of this bill. I think it is worth noting that when it was introduced by the then minister of justice, Hon. Davie Fulton, it was portrayed as being a rather hardy jewel which was being placed on the Conservative party crown of nationalism. The bill was brought in in 1962 after considerable delay, and at that time those of us who were in the house were somewhat surprised at the attitude of the official opposition, who put up as their main speaker and critic the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron). He gave the 20220-524
Corporations and Labour Unions Act house no indication that the official opposition was against the purpose of the bill but he did make some criticisms about specifics. Surprisingly enough the bill was debated for quite a long time, I think a total of about four days, and things became rather bitter between the minister as proponent and members of the opposition, including my colleague from the constituency of Skeena (Mr. Howard).
I have two points I want to make. First of all, the Conservatives presented this legislation as one of the most important pieces of legislation leading to the development of Canadian nationalism, particularly where corporations and trade unions were concerned. The official opposition's attitude was not critical, but it was never really explained whether that party was for it, was enthusiastic, or whatever the case was. However, I think it is fair to say that a certain amount of cynicism about the bill and the intentions of the government of that day was expressed by Liberal spokesmen, particularly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
Just to reinforce the emotion with which the bill was presented I should like to read a paragraph from Mr. Fulton's presentation, as reported at page 2396 of Hansard for April 2, 1962. He said:
This is an extremely important bill, and it forms an integral part of the government's national policy.
Those words "national policy" are fateful words, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) will acknowledge. Mr. Fulton went on:
Canadians are becoming increasingly aware of their nationhood and of the importance of developing to the full the cultural, social and economic resources of this country. This bill is directly related to the efforts the government has been making in such fields as the domiciling of our constitution in Canada, and also to the numerous steps the government has already taken, and is taking, to encourage the development of the nation's resources, their control by Canadians and their use primarily for the benefit of Canada.
In other words, this bill originally had a very noble purpose, I suppose part of the psychology was that by including all corporations above a certain level of revenue it would make them-particularly the ones that were foreign subsidiaries controlled from the United States-self-conscious about their Canadian operations, realizing that the government was looking at their shareholdings and the profits that were being taken out. This may have been a very good thing, but we do not know. Is it working? The minister gives
8268	HOUSE OF
Corporations and Labour Unions Act no indication at all that it has been useful in this regard.
One other point that was made in connection with the act, and I take this also from Mr. Fulton's statement, was referred to when he said in conclusion:
I should like to conclude with a few remarks as as to the policy of the bill. In the first place, as I have already stated, it is in a sense a first step. Second, it is designed to enable the government to understand the operations of the Canadian economy, an economy which admittedly owes much and will continue to owe much to foreign investment. However, no nation which calls itself sovereign can be careless of the extent of results of foreign control of vital segments of its economy. It is essential that we should at least understand careless of the extent or results of foreign control so that we may be able sensibly to determine the policies which should be followed in order to direct our own affairs as Canadians in the kind of world in which we live.
Again this was a very charming closing to the introductory speech to the bill.
The minister does not give us any indication at all that this act is working in this regard. All we really know or have is a report that was filed in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), which indicates that all the international and most Canadian unions have reported, and that some 20,000 odd corporations have also filed reports. I must say that I am delighted to know that that many corporations have complied with this act, because we heard Louis Lesage, the fellow who administers the Companies Act in another place, reveal something the other day that some of us found out a few years ago in so far as the Companies Act is concerned, and that is that the reports that are required by that act are being ignored by thousands and thousands of Canadian corporations.
This brings me to another point in relation to this bill, and again I am going to stress the fact that we have been given undertakings in this house-by the previous government I will agree-to the effect that the whole Companies Act was to be revised after interdepartmental discussion and after many meetings with provincial representatives so that, as Canadian chartered accountants and other business organizations wanted, we would join in having a common, rational and balanced company law throughout Canada. We have amendments coming from the other place at the present time to the Companies Act. At the time the original proposer of this bill proposed it, he suggested that this had been considered-that is, a change in the Companies Act to get this particular information-but it was felt that since the federal Companies 

Act did not sufficiently cover the corporations that needed to be considered, this could not be done at that time. I suggest if we are going to have a complete rewriting of the Companies Act, with standardization across the country, this is exactly the kind of thing that should be codified in co-operation with the provinces, so as to obtain this kind of information. That is why I wondered about these piecemeal small amendments at this time.
At the time of the original proposal the proposer said that the question had been considered of obtaining the information from the Department of National Revenue rather than having this report sent to the dominion statistician, but it was felt since the government was willing by this act to accept merely a copy of what was going to the Department of National Revenue, and since copying is very easy for corporate organizations-necessitating the use of Xerox machine-there was no real inconvenience, and the information could be largely identical, but it would go to the dominion bureau of statistics.
In the other place the dominion statistician suggested there is a great deal of duplication in terms of statistical analysis in this area. He pointed out that in respect of the taxation statistics that are published by the Department of National Revenue each year there is a duplication, and it is all punched out. This is not my understanding of the kind of information that was being sought. I cannot find any taxation statistics in Canada that give any real indication or understanding of the extent of foreign shareholdings in Canadian corporations. I cannot get from that information any indication as to the trends of shareholding or the amount of profit going to the parent organizations. Most of this kind of information I will admit should perhaps not be coming to me or any other individual, because this information probably is collected under clause 4(b) of the act.
However, I want to know whether the government really is getting and analysing this information. If we are merely by this amendment pawning off the right of the dominion statistician to look at the files or information collated by the Department of National Revenue, that is not good enough because the Department of National Revenue does not analyse this information from the point of view of the original purposes of this act.
This government is on record, largely through its Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), of being extremely vigilant. We remember the budget of 1963 and how terribly vigilant

the government was in repatriating Canadian ownership back into the Canadian financial community. Most of us can remember those provisions in the minister's budget of which he was so proud this afternoon, but which were wiped out very early. Why were they wiped out? I suggest they were wiped out because there was such an objection raised in respect of the changes that were going to affect United States ownership the government had to retreat. So far as I am aware the Minister of Finance has not retreated from his belief that one of the prime problems that faces the federal government of Canada is finding a method of obtaining a greater share in Canadian ownership, and finding out what we can do to reverse the trend.
One of the little games the Liberal spokesmen played when the Conservatives were in power was for them to point out that there was a trend toward greater United States ownership of Canadian resources, despite Conservative policy designed to put a stop to this and bring Canadian ownership back into the picture. I suppose we can now play that game and suggest that there is no indication at all that the Liberals have been able to stop this trend. Certainly the Minister of Finance backed down from his original approach to the matter. There has been a clear indication through the Minister of Finance that this government is as concerned as the previous one and in the same way, as indicated in those submissions put forward by E. Davie Fulton when he first presented the bill. That is why it is so hard to understand -unless the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not wish to put himself under the same blanket-why he would in a sense almost sneak in with these amendments. We have never had any real indication that the party now in government stands behind the original policy and purpose of this bill. We are no nearer to such an understanding, and that is why I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he says that this is something we deserve to know. We also deserve to know whether the shifting of information from the repository or files, if you want, of the dominion bureau of statistics, to the Department of National Revenue is really going to be satisfactory, and I must tell the minister that if he reads the evidence given before the committee of the other place by the dominion statistician I am sure he will find it is not an adequate explanation. It seemed to me as though the worthy gentle-20220-524i
Corporations and Labour Unions Act men were in a hurry to get on with it, and they did not bother to probe or ask questions.
It also raises another point which bothered me when the original bill came before the house. Why is it that the Senate gets the privilege of examining this legislation in committee and we do not? I cannot understand this. Maybe the idea is that since this piece of legislation relates to corporations and since the Senate is the old folks home for corporate directors it should be their particular prerogative and we "ickies" and "stupes" over here can really be bypassed. I do not think that is quite good enough. I should like to suggest that we should have a look at this bill in committee, inasmuch as a committee of the other place has had an opportunity to look at it.
I really do not feel that these amendments are of tremendous significance although they do have this significance. The bill is an indication that officialdom at least has lost its enthusiasm for cracking down and securing and using the information that was really intended to be sought. That is the first point. The second thing that is quite obvious is that the government is not enthusiastic about the bill as a whole, and I would assume that the legislation is going to waste away.
There are a couple of informational questions I should like to put to the minister. Will he let us see the forms that have been used in order to gather information under this act, or at the very least will he give us the notation in the Gazette where these forms were printed and published? The second thing I should like him to provide for me, and I hope for other members of the house, is the report that we were promised would follow from this legislation. I still have not seen it. Maybe I have missed it in my checking of sources. But I always understood that after the act had been operating for some time a thorough report would be presented together with an analysis of all the information that had been gathered. It was not going to be any really serious or consequential report because that would be ridiculous if you have 2,000 corporations reporting, but we certainly assumed that the information would be analysed, particularly with regard to trade unions.
For example, we have had Hal Banks and the S.I.U. on our minds for at least 15 or 16 months. The S.I.U. is an international union and I assume it has reported under this act. Maybe the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) can tell us. For example was any useful information with regard to Mr. Hal

Corporations and Labour Unions Act Banks' salary, his expense accounts and other reputed incomes revealed?
The point is that we have not been given the significance of the results that have been obtained under this act. Basically the purpose was to gather interesting statistics which I suppose were to give a psychological push to opening up information about Canadian ownership, perhaps to give both Canadian unions with international connections and Canadian companies under foreign domination or ownership an inkling that there was a trend or tide in affairs that must lead to greater Canadian participation in ownership, a declaration of our rights, if you will, in these two fields.
I feel that the minister has been completely inadequate in commenting on this legislation. We were not looking for a major speech, but at the very least he should have given us a succinct account. Perhaps he is all burnt out after his efforts over the week end. I must congratulate him on coming back to the house after his defeat with such a smile. I also see the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) over there. I think the minister could have done better than this.

speechtext:
Perhaps he could have done better in Toronto. I think he could have done better with his introduction of the bill. The last point I want to make in connection with this matter has been touched on by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). At the time the original legislation was introduced he was an interested onlooker because of his association with the labour movement. I happen to be one of the members who was in the house at the time and I had the very distinct impression that one of the reasons why we got this rather odd coupling of corporations and trade unions sponsored by the minister of justice of that time, and with the results to come to the dominion bureau of statistics, instead of trade unions being under the Department of Labour and corporations being under the Department of Finance or the Secretary of State, was that the government of the day felt that it would be the best way to get the thing through. If the corporation people kicked it could be pointed out that their rivals were getting it in the neck too, and vice-versa. Actually I think this was rather a successful ploy, if you will, because there was a tendency for corporations to

welcome information coming from trade unions and vice-versa.
I think the minister takes pride in being a reasonable man and a tidy administrator. I suggest he should give us his opinion whether he thinks the present act, even with these amendments made to it, is a tidy one. Is there not something rather silly about having trade unions reporting in this particular way and corporations reporting in this particular way, under the one act? It is not tidy and it is not sensible except in terms of some form of anti-Americanism. I do not see why a statute which will require statistical work and research should be set up on such an awkward basis.
There are all kinds of wiping away clauses in the bill. The railways do not have to report under this legislation. Why? Because they come under the Railway Act. Radio and television stations do not have to report because they come under such and such an act. I have a complaint about American ownership in Canadian broadcasting. I have a complaint about American ownership in the Canadian Pacific Railway. We do not know to what extent that exists. But if the purpose of the bill is to provide a continuing analysis of American ownership and control of corporations and trade unions, then I say let us bring all corporate organizations within its scope instead of having them split up and reporting under a whole host of acts. We are not really getting the information, so I suggest that in the interest of tidying things up and having proper administration you should put trade unions under the industrial relations act, or some of the other acts that come under the Minister of Labour, if you want this information from them; and if you need this information from corporations let us bring the reporting of all companies together, no matter what their operations may be, so that we can have a statistical analysis.
I put it to the minister that there is a television station for which his friend from Essex East used to be counsel-perhaps he still is-which everybody knows is 90 per cent owned by Americans. I assume that the statistics for that company are not covered by this act. How are we going to get a picture of the trend? The minister tells us that all he needs are summaries and that summaries will do the job. Obviously the summaries are incomplete. They must be incomplete because so many companies are not covered under the act, but under other legislation.

I suggest to the minister that he might even consider withdrawing the bill and tidying up the whole matter by some larger piece of legislation that would bring all information of this kind together, with corporations probably under the Department of Finance or reporting to some agency thereof and trade unions reporting to the Department of Labour. I have been carried away by my memories of the previous debate and have probably spoken too long, but I hope I have contributed, if not to the enlightenment of the minister, to the enlightenment of a few of my colleagues who may have forgotten the presentation that was made when the act was originally introduced.

maintopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FILING OF CORPORATION RETURNS
speechtext:
A reasonably comprehensive review of the legislation which is being amended has been given by several hon. members in this debate. However I believe the heart of the bill before us and of the amendment itself is contained in one clause, that is clause 4-I do not intend to deal with the various clauses-which adds section 14A to the act. In my view, Mr. Speaker, the addition of this one clause completely alters the whole purpose, intent and direction of this information act.
The original act, Mr. Speaker, as has been pointed out, was introduced in order to obtain certain information concerning non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada, labour unions with head offices outside of Canada, and so on. This information was believed to be necessary in order to obtain a broad picture of the operations of these non-resident companies, as well as resident companies and labour unions in Canada. The act, as passed in 1962, was very carefully drafted so that it would constitute no invasion of the privacy of income tax returns or other forms. Careful provision was made to ensure that no return should be made except to the dominion statistician and that that return should only have non-secret information in it, the type of information to which competitors, governments and others would be entitled in the normal course of business.
The present bill rearranges the whole purpose of the carefully designed original act because clause 4 will now permit an individual from the dominion statistician's office to go to the income tax office and examine the income tax return of any corporation in Canada under the guise of obtaining certain information. I believe this is a principle that has never been put forward before. I believe it is a breach of the confidentiality of income
Corporations and Labour Unions Act tax returns. In fact, what the government is saying in introducing this amendment is this: We are going to save you a little bit of trouble in filing those other returns; you will not have to file those special returns under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. We are going to examine your income tax return and take out of it what we want. This I believe, is the basis of the amendment. The whole principle is wrong and I am going to cast my vote against it unless there is some proposition made to refer this bill to a committee for amendment before it is given second reading.
I think that the principle in clause 4 is basically wrong. I could not possibly vote for it. Some people, like the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), may say that as soon as you mention corporation the members of the Conservative party jump to their defence. This is more serious than that, because it constitutes what is known as the thin edge of the wedge with regard to income tax returns. I should like, for example, to indicate what the passage of this amendment could do. Clause 14 permits the dominion statistician or any official described in subsection 4 of section 14 to inspect and have access to any return filed or made on behalf of any corporation pursuant to the Income Tax Act.
Now, you may say the information will not get beyond the dominion statistician's office or that the dominion statistician will not take any more information than he really needs. There is nothing in this act however to prevent that happening. This is particularly so in view of clause 14, subsection 5 of the original act which authorizes any official of the dominion statistician's office to obtain this information and to communicate it, (a) to another such person, that is a person such as himself or, (b), to allow any other person to inspect or have access to any statement or any writing containing any privileged information given under this act. These are the people who may give out any of this information. In effect therefore any corporation that has filed an income tax return is legally liable to have someone from the dominion statistician's office go and examine the income tax return, take out whatever the dominion statistician feels he needs for the purposes of this act, and he can then pass it on to any other person to whom he is inclined to give it.
This is carrying it too far. One of the things that has built up confidence in the administration of taxation measures in this country is the fact that the Department of National
8272	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Corporations and Labour Unions Act Revenue refuses to give out information contained in tax returns about the private affairs of a company which would be useful to its competitors or would be useful even to the crown in the right of the minister of justice on a criminal charge. The public in general, therefore, has extreme confidence in the confidentiality of their returns. These returns are filed accurately, or at least as accurately as one can hope, without any fear that someone is going to extract information from a return and make it public.
You may say that this is all done in a nice, accounting sort of way, that it is drawn up in tables and no company could be identified or picked out even if the dominion statistician wants to take more information than was originally allowed under this act. However there are many fields of endeavour in which a limited number of companies are engaged. This is just like the voting in some of our remote areas in which perhaps only one person votes. Certainly the secrecy of that particular vote is gone. Moreover if only three people vote and they all vote one way the secrecy of the vote is gone.
The situation is similar here. There must be many fields of business and manufacturing in this country in which there are limited numbers of people involved, and any return which showed more information than was strictly necessary could surely be traced back and be used in the manner I have mentioned. These are the things that are serious.
Moreover, this is a breach of the principles set out in the Income Tax Act where a penalty is provided for any person giving out confidential information to people who are not entitled to receive it. I presume that in addition such a person would be liable to dismissal. I should like to read from section 133 of the Income Tax Act which states, in relation to such communications:
Every person who while employed in the service of Her Majesty has communicated or allowed to be communicated to a person not legally entitled thereto any information obtained under this act-
And so on. I stress the words "not legally entitled thereto" because if we pass these amendments the dominion statistician, any officials employed by him or any person to whom the dominion statistician chooses to give this information in the line of duty would be legally entitled to it under section 14 of the act we now have under consideration. In other words, under the guise of making this information easier to provide by the companies concerned we are relaxing the secrecy provisions beyond anything intended in the In-

come Tax Act and we are not preserving the confidentiality which in Canada we have always been led to expect would attach to income tax returns.
As I said a moment ago, I do not think we have given sufficient consideration to the effect of clause 14. The provisions of the rest of the bill do not appear to be dangerous or damaging. Alternative ways of making the returns are provided. The requirement with regard to signatories has been altered, and so on. All this is inconsequential. But clause 14 does, I believe, constitute a serious invasion of privacy and a relaxation of the secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act far beyond what was intended. For these reasons I believe the act should be given further consideration and that we should receive much fuller explanation before it is passed as presented. I know that a number of my friends are prepared to speak on this and that they will give the measure all kinds of consideration. As far as I am concerned, though, I will have to vote against it if the motion comes to a vote.

maintopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FILING OF CORPORATION RETURNS
speechtext:
This seemingly innocuous measure presented to us by the government is not, in my opinion, nearly as innocuous as it would appear from the remarks of the minister who introduced it. I think the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) echoed a feeling which must be widespread in the house when he said there had not been sufficient explanation of this desire for change in the method of obtaining information.
The first question which occurs to me is: Do we still want the information which the government desired to acquire when this act was passed in 1962. I should also like to know whether we got that information or not. Has any use been made of it? Was that information of any help to the government in formulating its present policies? I think it is a good idea for us to recall that there was a good deal of debate in the house when this legislation was first considered. Many arguments were advanced to show why this information could not be obtained from ordinary income tax returns. Some of the dangers of such a course were pointed out, and I do not think the government has answered the valid arguments, which at that time were accepted substantially by everyone, in favour of this special method of getting certain information which the government desired to have from these companies.
At that time there was perhaps more immediate concern about the domination of Canadian companies by United States enter-

prises. We were perhaps more urgently aware of balance of payments difficulties. Certain union questions were also more pressing and urgent than they are today. But I would feel much happier if the government would now take a stand and tell us why they want to change this bill which was passed in 1962. Possibly the government will tell us that they are no longer worried about United States domination of Canadian companies. Has the situation changed to such an extent that Canadians are now putting up the degree of finance we should all like to see? Has the percentage of foreign ownership and control of our companies declined to such an extent that this is no longer a question which need make us uneasy?
I do not think any member of this house would deny that the underlying reason for bringing in this legislation was concern over the degree of foreign ownership and control of Canadian companies. There was a feeling among members of the government, shared throughout the country, that the excessive domination of our companies by firms abroad was not healthy for Canada. There had been instances of Canadian companies owned by United States companies showing little enthusiasm for taking up opportunities to export to communist dominated nations. Again, certain Canadian companies in a position to compete in markets overseas were being held up because their parent companies preferred to see United States firms dominating exports to those areas. But today we have not heard one word from the government that this situation has changed in any respect.
No one argues that merely getting this information will cure a situation of the kind I have outlined. But the essence of the reason for passing this act in 1962 was that before these problems could be adequately dealt with and before the public could exercise proper judgment as to the seriousness of the situation, complete information had to be acquired. It was argued, successfully, that in order to acquire this information specific targets had to be set out and specific questions answered so as to provide details which would bear little relation to those given in the income tax returns normally filed by these companies. I think the government owes the house an explanation why this principle has been abandoned. What is this sense of well being, this sense of security, which has brought about a change in the government's attitude? Does the government no longer care whether our companies are under foreign control, or is the situation no longer what it was two
Corporations and Labour Unions Act or three years ago? Is there some dark reason behind this change? Has the government been approached by representatives of foreign dominated companies who say: "This is too embarrassing. If you want our continued good will you must let us off the hook"?
I suggest these proposed amendments do constitute a fundamental change in philosophy. This being so, the government should be prepared to tell us why it has changed its attitude. What has disappeared from the picture? Why is the question of foreign control no longer of interest? I think the government should also tell us something about the way in which this act has worked during the last two years, roughly.
Is it a situation where certain people charged with the statistical compilation of this information, those people who received these returns and were supposed to put them in a form that would be useful to the government and to the public, have failed to put the information in this form? Was there any lack of enthusiasm in some of these departments to compile this sort of information? Has it just been allowed to sit and gather dust, as is usually the case with so much information collected by the government? If it has been adequately handled, and if the respective civil servants in those departments have had put into their hands the type of information that the government thought necessary in 1962, what can the government now tell us with regard to what has been revealed by that information? What does it amount to? What is the position of foreign control and foreign domination now? What are the long term trends in this respect? Is there any substantial increase in investment by Canadian workers and shareholders?
Next, Mr. Speaker, if that information has been correlated and put into the form in which it was envisaged it would be used, what help has it been? Has it had any influence on government thinking? Has it had any influence on the methods this government might be working on to induce Canadians to invest more in Canadian companies? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these are very simple questions and deserve answers. Certainly the hon. member for Port Arthur revealed the lack of knowledge that lay behind his own bewilderment with regard to this legislation. If we are going to make a change that is so fundamental, with regard to a question decided only two years ago by this whole house, and which was accepted as sensible and necessary at that time, what are the logical reasons for making that change?
8274	HOUSE OF
Corporations and Labour Unions Act Surely this is not too much to ask the minister.
I do not want to go over the ground covered by some other hon. members, but I thought the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) had a good point when he asked, why not send it to a committee? That suggestion was echoed by the hon. member for Port Arthur. The Senate thought it necessary. If I am correct in my assertion that this is really a very fundamental change in policy, it might not hurt at all if the banking and commerce committee of this house took a long, searching look at it. Perhaps the explanation the minister would like to give, or the information revealed by those statistics already filed, is so complicated and of such a nature that it is impracticable for the minister to attempt at this time to give us a breakdown which we can examine. Perhaps it has not been refined enough that it can be presented in any simple manner to this house. Certainly if that is the case I think this is the sort of function for which a committee of this house is designed. That is exactly what the committee can do. Present that information to the committee, let them study it, refine it and see whether it has been helpful. I suggest that any change now of what was thought so logical, when there is no evidence presented that it has been unsuccessful or unnecessary, warrants an explanation being given to the house. There has not even been a suggestion by the minister that it is not still needed. The present action is substantiated by no logical argument that I can think of.
Certainly if you are going to test a method and see whether it works, you have to present some evidence if you want to change it. You must show that you have tried it, that you have tested it, and you must put forward some evidence that it does not work. Perhaps the method of collecting the information that was originally envisaged in this act is the best. If it is not, this house, or at least a committee of the house, has a right to look into the matter before we are asked to change that method. We have the right to look at the efforts that were made to compile this information, to assess it, and to look at the results achieved to see what has been accomplished. I suggest to the minister that until that old method-I say "old", although it is only two years old-can by any of these time tested methods be proven to be wrong, he has no logical reason for asking us to change it now.


I listened to the hon. member for Simcoe North and his suggestion that this is an extension of the powers of looking at income tax returns. I think it is more than that. There was a distinction under the old method which will not apply now. This only applied to large corporations with assets of $500,000 or so, which were required to make these special returns. However, Mr. Speaker, unless I have overlooked something, the income tax department will now have the right to look at the returns of all companies.
Since, in the absence of words from the minister to the contrary, we can imagine that the people in the bureau of vital statistics who are going to look at these returns are going to be looking for the same things, I imagine there will be pressure from that bureau on the income tax branch to amend the income tax return form so that it will give more complete information. I do not think this is exaggeration in any sense. It is going to subject more companies, smaller companies, to the searching glance of the statisticians; but it will also cause pressure to be brought to bear on the income tax department to amend their returns in a manner that will satisfy the needs of the bureau of statistics and the government for further information.
My memory may be faulty, but it seems to me these were exactly the arguments we used in 1962-that since the purposes were not the same, and since there was really a very narrow purpose behind the returns required, we would be most unwise to upset the income tax department, their method of reporting and their need for secrecy, by mixing in the special request of the government for special statistics affecting the general health of the nation in regard to the question of foreign domination and control. I for one will be very happy if the minister can show that my memory is very faulty in this regard, or if he can reveal sufficient evidence to show this house that the method of collecting information which we set up only two years ago has fallen down completely, or that the government has fallen down completely in the various departments in making use of this information, or that conditions in the country are such that any information on foreign ownership, control and domination of Canadian companies is no longer of concern. I hope that if the minister's reply on this matter is necessarily a long and involved one, he will take the easy course of sending it to a committee, where we will be prepared to examine it at leisure and with an open mind, hoping to be convinced.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act I think I can be brief. I was impressed by the last speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) and also by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) both of whom suggested that this bill be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce, a committee of parliament. Perhaps the question being asked by most speakers is, why the amendment at all? I do not think the minister has clarified why there should be an amendment. It is obvious that the minister does not want one: It is the officials-I have always felt this- who are behind the minister, whether he be a Conservative minister or a Liberal minister, who are not satisfied with the material they are getting either from labour unions or corporations. Therefore they want the act amended so they can get this information they are looking for.
The second point which impresses me, a point referred to by one of the speakers, is that when we open up the gate to a department, in this case the Department of National Revenue, we are opening up a new field of law-and a very dangerous field of law, when we go into income tax returns. Because the minister has not explained to the house why he requires this particular fork to be put into the act to dig up the proper information, and because he has not explained why he needs to go into a new field and enable another department to go into income tax returns-which is, I suggest, a very dangerous trend, the end of which we will never know -I am myself unhappy about this bill.
All who have spoken so far have agreed that in order to find out who has control of our labour unions or corporations this information should be provided; there is no argument
Corporations and Labour Unions Act there. I need only refer to what was said by the hon. member for Port Arthur regarding the S.I.U.; we know the kind of control which was held in that case. I suppose I could also name corporations on the other side of the fence which would be just as interesting factually as was the S.I.U. Therefore I am going to move-and I said I would be short- on those two counts, and because I have been impressed by what these hon. members have said, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken):
That the bill be not now read a second time but that the contents thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a point of order on this amendment. I understand that on second reading of a bill it is inadmissible to move that a bill itself go to a standing committee. The wording of the amendment obviously means that it is the bill itself that is to be sent to the committee because it refers to the "contents" of the bill. The standard form for moving such an amendment is to refer the subject matter, which is entirely different. I suggest that this amendment is not in order.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):

maintopic: FARM MACHINERY
subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister, who is out of the country on government business, I wish to make a statement on second reading of this bill. The minister appreciated the constructive criticism and remarks of members of the house, the concern they expressed with regard to the bill and the interest they have taken in it. I ask the indulgence of the house to permit me to stick to my script because
Farm Machinery
I wish to be rather precise, since I am speaking for the minister.
A number of questions were asked concerning the proposals which would be contained in the bill and how this proposed credit program would operate. An examination of the bill itself will provide the answer to most of these questions.
The government has been concerned, and hon. members have indicated their concern, about the cost to Canadian farmers of owning and operating farm machinery. As an indication of the size of this problem I should like to point out that at the time of the 1961 census the value of farm machinery on farms in Canada amounted to more than $2J billion. During 1963 the cost to Canadian farmers for owning and operating their machinery amounted to about $541 million and more than half of these costs were represented by the cost of ownership, including depreciation and interest on investment. When we consider ways of increasing the farmer's income I am sure we are all thinking of his net income. Anything which we can do to reduce the farmer's operating costs is in effect a move to improve his income.
As the minister indicated in his remarks at the resolution stage, the co-operative use of farm machinery is already practised among Canadian farmers by sharing in the ownership of individual machines or by having work done on a custom basis.
Two factors have made more extensive cooperative use of machinery difficult. The first has been the need for the determination and establishment of a simple and workable basis for the organization of co-operative groups of farmers. The second has been the lack of adequate credit facilities to enable such groups to operate. The purpose of this bill is to assist in overcoming these two problems and, in this manner, to encourage joint ownership by groups of farmers of these types of machinery and equipment, the use of which may be shared in order to reduce the overhead costs of each farmer.
For this reason, the bill proposes to set up what has been termed syndicates. The syndicates in effect will be groups of three or more persons engaged in farming who have entered into a form of partnership agreement with one another to undertake the joint purchase and use of farm machinery. The bill is designed to assist those whose principal occupation is farming. However, because of location and other factors, it may be very much to the advantage of some full-time farmers to include in their syndicate neigh-

Farm Machinery
hours who are farming but also engaged in other pursuits. The bill provides for this kind of co-operation, but to assure that full time farmers are the chief beneficiaries at least the majority of members of any syndicate must be persons whose main occupation is farming.
There has been some question of the choice of the word "syndicate" to identify these groups. A syndicate by definition means a combination of persons formed for the promotion of an enterprise. There are, of course, other terms which might have been used, and in fact were considered. Some speakers have suggested the word "co-operative". This word was considered, but there is now legislation in practically every province for the formal incorporation of co-operatives, and we did not think it wise to use a term which might seem to conflict with provincial jurisdiction.
The word "syndicate" is an appropriate one to define a combination of persons formed to promote an enterprise or for the acquisition of articles. In fact the use of the word "syndicates" for this purpose is by no means new in Canada. In the early days of the west the term "syndicate" was widely used to describe groups of farmers who joined together for the purchase of machinery.
Several members pointed out, quite properly, that some items of farm machinery lend themselves to joint ownership and use, but there are other items which a farmer has to own himself if he is to be sure of having them available when he needs them most.
There will be authority in the bill to define farm machinery by regulation. We thought it best to do it in this way because we are entering into a completely new venture in which we will have to profit by experience, and in which some changes may be required as we gain experience. The intention, however, would be to define farm machinery very broadly, so that the bill might apply to any item of machinery which a farmer might use in the development or operation of his farm, and leave it to the groups as they are organized to decide the items which they feel could profitably be owned and used jointly.
The bill proposes loans up to 80 per cent of the cost to the syndicate of the machinery which they buy. The remaining 20 per cent of the cost, spread between the various members of the syndicate, will allow individuals to become members with a relatively small initial contribution. The maximum amount

of loans to any one syndicate would be $15,000 per member, but not to exceed $100,000. These amounts should be sufficient to allow syndicates to share in the purchase of a considerable amount of equipment, including those specialized items of high capital cost which are available for use but which are too expensive for farmers to purchase on an individual basis.
The initial organization of the syndicates is most important for their future success. Farmers wishing to organize to take advantage of the provisions of this bill will require some assistance and guidance in their initial planning. The minister is proposing that the responsibility for the administration of the measure be assigned to the Farm Credit Corporation so that we may make use of the facilities which they have already established across the county and the experience they have gained in administering farm credit.
It is proposed also to make the program self-supporting. One of the principal items of cost will be the initial establishing of the syndicate, the study of its proposal, and the approval of the loan. This is provided for by a service charge of 1 per cent of the amount of the loan. The cost of administering the loan, once it is made, will be provided for in the interest rates which will be fixed from time to time by the corporation with the approval of the governor in council.
Mr. Speaker, there is quite a bit of chattering in the house. I had hoped that this bill would commend itself to the members sufficiently that they may wish to listen to the statement.
In this connection, I should like to point out that since these loans will be for terms not exceeding seven years, the cost of the money to the corporation will be less than the cost of money it borrows for the making of long term loans under the Farm Credit Act. I am informed that within recent years the cost of money borrowed for periods of less than ten years has been about half of 1 per cent less than the cost of money borrowed for periods of up to 20 years.
Since this is a new type of program there will undoubtedly be problems to overcome in its initial operation. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) has mentioned in particular the difficulties which may arise when several farmers endeavour to share the use of one particular machine. In drafting the provisions of the bill, and planning for its administration, consideration has been given

to the ways in which these problems can be lessened.
The first essential factor, of course, is the compatibility of the members one with another, and since syndicates will be formed on the initiative of individual farmers who choose their own partners to participate with them I have no doubt that farmers will find partners with whom they can work amicably. Further, in the setting up of the syndicate there will be predetermined arrangements designed to settle in advance some of the problems which may later arise. There will first be some general provisions applicable to all syndicates, including such items as provisions for adding members, for reduction in membership, for the procedure in the event of death or insolvency of a member, and for the voluntary dissolution of the syndicate. There will also be provisions for such items as the appointment of a secretary, the maintenance of proper books of account, and so on.
Farmers forming syndicates will also be required to make arrangements in advance concerning their individual shares and responsibilities with respect to payment of capital maintenance and operating costs, and the responsibilities for operation, repair, maintenance and storage of the machines. They will need to agree concerning the priority of the right to use the machine in the event that two members wish to use it at the same time. By agreeing on this type of thing in advance many of the difficulties of co-operative use will be overcome.
It is appreciated that the provisions of this bill do not apply equally well to all types of machinery and equipment. Syndicates formed to purchase harvesting equipment, for example, where the time at which the farmer has the machine available is of vital importance, will probably contain a relatively limited number of members. It will be important to ensure when the syndicate is being formed that the machinery being purchased has ample capacity to meet the requirements of all the members within the season of use. However, in dealing with such machinery as that used for land clearing, land levelling, drainage, etc., it may be possible to form syndicates with larger numbers of farmers because the time of use of the equipment is not such a vital factor.
I might point out also that a farmer who obtains assistance under this bill would still retain his eligibility for loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act for equipment he wishes to purchase on his own, as well as for livestock, building improvements, etc.
Farm Machinery
Hon. members may wish to have some information with respect to this type of operation elsewhere. Syndicates of the type proposed in this bill were started as a pilot project in the United Kingdom in 1955 and developed slowly during the first few years. By 1962, 293 syndicates had been formed. However, as a result of the program's successful operations it has expanded rapidly since that time. In 1963 there were 341 syndicates and by August of this year, 596 syndicates had been formed. Farmers who are members of syndicates who were interviewed concerning their operations indicate that disagreements among syndicate members are rare. They indicated, for example, that the problem of three small farmers deciding upon the order in which a machine should be used by each was not very different from that of a large farmer deciding upon the order in which he would use a machine in his own fields, and the problem was usually resolved after consideration of the same factors as those which influence the decision of the larger farmer. It is interesting to note, also, that some of these syndicates have found it advantageous to share their labour resources as well as their machinery.
It has been suggested that this legislation will be of more value to large operators. On the contrary I believe the advantages of cooperative use are far more significant to the small operator. It may be a perfectly economic proposition for a large farmer to own equipment large and efficient enough to do all his work, while such a proposal might be beyond the means of the small farmer. The opportunity provided to a syndicate to acquire machinery, with an initial payment of 20 per cent of the cost spread among three, four or five members will make it possible for small farmers with limited capital resources to share in the ownership of efficient machinery for operating their land with low individual investment and overhead.
As I have already indicated, this bill is a new departure to meet a new and expanding need for credit and co-operation among farmers. It is designed to assist them to reduce their machinery costs. It proposes a fund of $25 million to meet the initial demand. I have no doubt that after the act is in full operation experience will indicate some changes and modifications and perhaps the need for a larger fund. In this event, amendments will be introduced to make such improvements. But I believe we have in this present bill all the fundamentals of a practical program which will offer very real assistance to Canadian
